analysis.one_liner: Extends federal price supports for wheat, corn, oilseeds, sugar, honey, and wool.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee with four cosponsors in April 1990 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lock in federal farm price support programs for five more years. Farmers of wheat, corn, soybeans, and other crops would get government loans at guaranteed minimum prices plus direct 'deficiency payments' when market prices fall below set floors. Sugar, honey, and wool growers would keep their own support programs. The money comes from taxpayers, and the sugar floor keeps domestic sugar prices above world levels, which shows up in food prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of the supported commodities: wheat and feed grain growers (guaranteed loan rates of at least $2.75/bushel for wheat and $2.10 for corn, plus deficiency payments tied to an established price of $4.00 for wheat and $2.75 for corn), oilseed and soybean growers (new recourse loans at $6.25/bushel for soybeans), sugar growers (a minimum 18-cent-per-pound cane sugar loan rate, with authority to raise it), and honey and wool/mohair growers, all through the 1995 crop year. Payments scale with acreage and yield, so larger operations collect the most. The bill also protects tenants and sharecroppers' shares of payments and adds optional conservation and public-access incentives.

how_it_helps.text: Sets guaranteed minimum government loan rates for wheat ($2.75/bushel) and corn ($2.10/bushel) and minimum 'established prices' of $4.00 and $2.75 that trigger deficiency payments when markets fall short, through the 1995 crops [S2][S3].
Creates new five-year oilseed loans ($6.25/bushel for soybeans) and extends wool, mohair, sugar, and honey support programs through 1995 [S2][S3].

Adds disaster payments for prevented planting and reduced yields when crop insurance does not cover the loss, and lets producers plant flexible mixes of program crops and oilseeds without losing their payment base [S2][S3].
Requires safeguards so tenants and sharecroppers receive their fair share of program payments, and offers extra payments to farmers who open diverted land to public hunting, fishing, and hiking [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the loans, deficiency payments, and disaster payments through the Commodity Credit Corporation. Consumers pay more for sugar than they would at world prices, because the bill sets a support floor of 18 cents per pound for cane sugar and authorizes increases based on producers' costs, and the sugar program operates through import and marketing controls. Livestock feeders and food processors face higher grain and sugar input costs when acreage reduction programs tighten supply.

drawbacks.text: The sugar title sets a minimum loan rate of 18 cents per pound for raw cane sugar and lets the Secretary raise it based on domestic production costs, which keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels and raises costs for consumers and sugar-using food makers [S3].

The bill extends five more crop years of taxpayer-funded deficiency payments, diversion payments, and disaster payments across every major program commodity, with the bill's own stock-goal section acknowledging that surplus levels directly drive taxpayer cost [S2][S3].
It renews the wool and mohair price support program through 1995, a program long criticized for paying producers far more than the market value of the wool and mohair sold [S2].

It drops cross-compliance, letting a producer qualify for wheat or feed grain payments without participating in other commodity programs, which increases program complexity and can raise total subsidy costs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives real income security to farmers facing volatile prices, and its flexibility and conservation provisions are genuinely useful. But the benefits are concentrated among producers of a handful of supported commodities — and skew toward the largest operations, since payments follow acreage and yield — while the costs are spread across every taxpayer and added to food prices through the sugar floor. It is a continuation of a subsidy structure rather than a reform of it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the Congress ended with it still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator Kerrey introduced the bill on April 3, 1990, joined by original cosponsors Daschle, Harkin, Conrad, and Exon [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — the bill never left the committee and died there when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and food consumers are better off that this version never advanced, since it would have extended five years of commodity subsidies and an 18-cent sugar floor. Commodity producers did not go away empty-handed: Congress passed a separate 1990 farm bill that fall, which is widely reported, though on different terms than this bill.

for.name: Sen. J. Robert Kerrey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Farm Income and Flexibility Act of 1990 and became its sole sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Daschle, Harkin, Conrad, and Exon
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; all five Senate supporters were Democrats, but the bill also died in a committee whose majority was Democratic, and a separate 1990 farm bill passed instead.

industries.industry: Grain producers (wheat, corn, barley, oats, sorghum)
industries.note: The bill guarantees them minimum loan rates and deficiency payments for five crop years, funded by taxpayers. Payments follow acreage and yield, so large grain operations capture the biggest share.
The bill locks in the sugar price support program through 1995 with an 18-cent-per-pound floor on cane sugar, a program that keeps domestic sugar prices above world levels at consumer expense.
New five-year recourse loans at set minimums give them a price floor financed through the Commodity Credit Corporation.
Extends their price support program through 1995; the program has long been criticized for paying far more than the market value of the fiber.
The bill extends the honey price support program at a 56.86-cent-per-pound minimum through 1995.

industries.industry: Livestock feeders and sugar-using food processors
industries.note: Acreage reduction programs and the sugar support floor raise the cost of feed grains and sugar these industries buy, costs that pass through to food prices.
